title: Japan Air Lines Flight 123
one_line: An incorrectly repaired pressure wall failed, damaging the tail and controls before a mountain crash.
status_why: Wreckage and flight recordings support the repair failure explanation; questions remain about rescue decisions and why the repair went wrong.

aircraft.livery_notes: The 1984 photograph in s13 shows a white upper fuselage and fin, silver-grey lower fuselage, red and dark window stripes, dark JAPAN AIR LINES titles, and a red crane/JAL tail emblem. Exact accident-day decals and paint condition were not verified.

site.description: Osutaka-no-one, the crash ridge northwest of Mount Mikuni in the Mount Takamagahara area, Ueno, Gunma; not the summit of Mount Osutaka. Section 2.1 gives 35°59′54″N 138°41′49″E. The decimal location here assumes Tokyo Datum and applies the approximate conversion described in s8. Sections 2.1 and 2.3 both give about 1,565 m, about 5,135 ft. Earlier contacts were at the single-larch ridge and the U-shaped ditch.

terrain_box.why: Display choice, not an evidential boundary: about 59 km east-west by 44 km north-south around the final mountain path, Mount Mikuni, the impact ridges and the rescue approaches.

events.title: Earlier tail strike
events.detail: On 2 June 1978, the aircraft struck its aft fuselage during landing at Osaka. The aft pressure bulkhead and surrounding structure were damaged.
events.caption: An earlier landing damaged the rear fuselage and the wall that holds cabin pressure.

events.title: Boeing repairs the aircraft
events.detail: A Boeing team repaired the aircraft at Haneda between 17 June and 11 July 1978. At part of the bulkhead splice, the work differed from the instruction and left a single effective rivet row; inspectors did not identify the error.
events.caption: An incorrect repair left part of the pressure wall's joint weakened. Inspectors missed the error.

events.title: Flight leaves the stand
events.detail: The captain sat in the right seat while the first officer trained for command from the left seat. Flight 123 taxied from stand 18.
events.caption: The flight taxied out with the first officer training for command and the captain in the right seat.

events.title: Takeoff roll begins
events.detail: The DFDR identifies the start of the takeoff roll.
events.caption: The aircraft began its takeoff run.

events.title: Aircraft lifts off
events.detail: The aircraft departed Haneda runway 15L for Osaka.
events.caption: The aircraft took off from Haneda for Osaka.

events.title: Direct route approved
events.detail: Tokyo Control approved a direct route to Seaperch while the aircraft climbed toward 24,000 ft.
events.caption: Controllers approved a direct route to Seaperch as the aircraft climbed.

events.title: Loud sound and structural failure
events.detail: A loud sound was recorded near the start of the abnormal motion. The investigation inferred failure of the repaired bulkhead, followed by damage to the aft fuselage and vertical fin.
events.caption: A loud sound accompanied unusual movement. The repaired pressure wall likely failed, damaging the rear fuselage and tail.

events.title: Acceleration spike recorded
events.detail: The longitudinal acceleration showed an abrupt forward spike. The report uses it with other recorder channels to reconstruct the structural sequence.
events.caption: The aircraft abruptly accelerated forward.

events.title: Autopilot command mode ends
events.detail: The DFDR recorded autopilot command mode switching off.
events.caption: The autopilot switched off.

events.title: Crew requests return to Haneda
events.detail: The captain requested descent to 22,000 ft and return to Haneda.
events.caption: The captain requested a descent and a return to Haneda.

events.title: Right turn instruction acknowledged
events.detail: The crew acknowledged a right turn toward magnetic heading 090 for vectors via Oshima. The aircraft did not follow the intended return route.
events.caption: The crew acknowledged instructions to turn right, but the aircraft did not follow the intended return route.

events.title: Large oscillations develop
events.detail: The DFDR commentary identifies pronounced phugoid and Dutch-roll motion from about this time. Control inputs did not suppress it after hydraulic control was lost.
events.caption: The aircraft began repeatedly climbing, descending, and swaying. The controls could not stop this after hydraulic control failed.

events.title: Rescue center receives emergency notice
events.detail: Tokyo Airport rescue coordination began collecting information after notification of the aircraft emergency.
events.caption: Rescue coordinators began gathering information about the aircraft's emergency.

events.title: Crew reports loss of control
events.detail: The captain told Tokyo Control that the aircraft was uncontrollable.
events.locator: Section 2.1, printed p.7; Attachment 6, PDF p.299
events.caption: The captain told controllers the aircraft could not be controlled.

events.title: Nagoya offered as an option
events.detail: Tokyo Control gave the distance to Nagoya and asked whether the crew could land there. The crew again requested Haneda.
events.locator: Section 2.1, printed p.7; Attachment 6, PDF p.302
events.caption: Controllers offered Nagoya as a landing option. The crew again requested Haneda.

events.title: Oxygen masks discussed
events.detail: The flight engineer urged use of oxygen masks. The report found no evidence that the flight crew wore them and considered some hypoxic impairment possible; this was an inference, not a medical measurement.
events.caption: The flight engineer urged oxygen mask use. It is unclear whether the flight crew wore them.

events.title: Main landing gear extends
events.detail: Main landing gear extension was recorded.
events.caption: The main landing gear extended.

events.title: Local sunset
events.detail: The report gives sunset at the crash site as about 18:40 JST.
events.caption: The sun set at the crash site at about 6:40 p.m.

events.title: Engine power is reduced
events.detail: EPR decreased substantially and the descent rate increased.
events.caption: Engine power fell substantially, and the aircraft descended faster.

events.title: Haneda vectors requested again
events.detail: The crew requested radar vectors to Haneda. Tokyo Control directed heading 090 and advised runway 22.
events.caption: The crew again requested directions to Haneda. Controllers gave an eastward heading and a runway.

events.title: Radar becomes unreliable
events.detail: Mountain interference increasingly disrupted radar returns. Investigators reconstructed the later path mainly from DFDR integration.
events.caption: Mountains increasingly disrupted radar tracking of the aircraft.

events.title: Minimum calibrated airspeed recorded
events.detail: DFDR commentary gives 108 kt calibrated airspeed and angle of attack 30.9 degrees. These are not a groundspeed or an IAS measurement.
events.caption: Airspeed reached its recorded minimum of 108 knots, with the wing at a steep angle to the airflow.

events.title: Flap extension begins
events.detail: Leading-edge groups began extending, except the outer groups. The main text gives a slightly different time for the beginning of continuing flap operation.
events.caption: Movable panels along the wings' front edges began extending, except those on the outer sections.

events.title: Leading-edge extension completes
events.detail: The recorded leading-edge groups completed extension, with the outer groups still excluded.
events.caption: The panels along the wings' front edges finished extending, except those on the outer sections.

events.title: Crew asks its position
events.detail: Tokyo Approach supplied the aircraft position relative to Haneda and Kumagaya. This spoken fix is not entered as an exact coordinate.
events.caption: The crew asked their position. Controllers described where the aircraft was relative to Haneda and Kumagaya.

events.title: Haneda and Yokota offered
events.detail: Tokyo Approach advised that both airports were available. This was not a completed approach or a demonstrated ability to reach either runway.
events.caption: Controllers told the crew that both Haneda and Yokota were available for landing.

events.title: Flap retraction starts
events.detail: The main text places the flaps at about 25 units and the start of retraction here; Attachment 5 gives 18:55:42. Right bank increased further.
events.locator: Section 3.1.7.4, printed p.79; Attachment 5, PDF p.292
events.caption: The flaps began retracting as the aircraft tilted farther to the right.

events.title: Steep descent develops
events.detail: The aircraft pitched down and power was increased. The report places it at about 10,000 ft pressure altitude.
events.caption: The aircraft's nose dropped into a steep descent, and engine power increased.

events.title: Aircraft crashes on the ridge
events.detail: The report gives the overall crash time as approximately 18:56. Contact events and the last recorder values establish a sequence within that minute, but no exact final-rest time is asserted here.
events.caption: The aircraft crashed on the ridge at about 6:56 p.m. The exact time it stopped is unknown.

events.title: Nose-down attitude reaches thirty-six degrees
events.detail: The DFDR commentary gives about 36 degrees nose down and about 70 degrees right bank.
events.caption: The aircraft pointed about 36 degrees nose down and tilted about 70 degrees to the right.

events.title: Ground warning and recovery attempt
events.detail: The report relates ground-proximity warning activation to increased power and a temporary arrest of descent. Its two altitude descriptions disagree.
events.locator: Section 3.1.7.4, printed p.80; Attachment 5, PDF p.292
events.caption: A warning sounded about nearby ground. Engine power increased, and the descent briefly stopped.

events.title: Right wing contacts trees
events.detail: Recorder changes and wreckage support an initial right-wing contact near the single-larch ridge. The report infers separation of the No.4 engine.
events.caption: The right wing struck trees near a ridge. The outer right engine likely broke away.

events.title: Contact at the U-shaped ditch
events.detail: The investigation associates a second contact sound and acceleration changes with the ridge containing the U-shaped ditch. The aircraft then continued toward the main crash ridge.
events.caption: The aircraft struck another ridge, then continued toward the main crash ridge.

events.title: Last analysable attitude recorded
events.detail: The last analysable set gives pitch minus 42.2 degrees, right roll 131.5 degrees, magnetic heading 277.1 degrees and calibrated airspeed 263.7 kt.
events.caption: The final flight recorder reading shows the nose steeply down and the aircraft rolled beyond vertical.

events.title: Radar disappearance reported to rescuers
events.detail: The rescue center received notice that the radar target had disappeared at about 18:57. The radar-loss report time is not the impact time.
events.caption: Rescue coordinators received notice that the aircraft had disappeared from radar.

events.title: Japanese fighters launch
events.detail: Two standby jets were dispatched to locate the aircraft.
events.caption: Two Japanese fighter jets took off to search for the aircraft.

events.title: US C-130 reports fire
events.detail: A US Air Force C-130 reported a fire at Yokota TACAN radial 305, 35 NM. JTSB later plotted an approximately 3 km position error for this report.
events.caption: A US military transport aircraft reported a fire, but its reported position was about three kilometers off.

events.title: Fighters report flames
events.detail: Two F-4EJs reported flames using a different TACAN fix. JTSB later plotted an approximately 6 km error.
events.caption: Two fighter jets reported flames, but their reported position was about six kilometers off.

events.title: Japanese helicopter observes flames
events.detail: A Japanese rescue helicopter reached the area and reported another position. JTSB later plotted an approximately 4 km error.
events.caption: A Japanese rescue helicopter observed flames, but its reported position was about four kilometers off.

events.title: Antonucci recalls return order
events.detail: In his 1995 account, the C-130 navigator said a Marine helicopter could not land in smoke and flame, but offered to lower crew nearby. He recalled a command-post order for both aircraft to return because Japanese rescuers were coming; contemporaneous US orders were not obtained.
events.locator: s12 printed pp.5-6, edited reproduction of 1995 account
events.caption: A US navigator later recalled orders to return despite a helicopter's offer to lower rescuers nearby.

events.title: Night guidance attempt fails
events.detail: JTSB describes a helicopter attempt to guide prefectural police from the air as unsuccessful. Its plotted location was about 2 km from the site.
events.caption: A helicopter's attempt to guide police from the air failed, about two kilometers from the crash site.

events.title: Military search reports wreckage
events.detail: The 1987 report describes wreckage discovery and site confirmation at this time. The later JTSB location table still places the reported location about 3 km away.
events.caption: Military searchers reported finding wreckage, but their reported position was about three kilometers from the crash site.

events.title: Police helicopter confirms the site
events.detail: A Nagano Prefectural Police helicopter identified the crash site.
events.caption: A police helicopter identified the crash site.

events.title: Survivors are found
events.detail: Rescuers found survivors among wreckage in the third branch of Sugeno Dale. The four survivors had been seated in the aft cabin.
events.caption: Rescuers found four survivors among the wreckage. All had been seated in the rear cabin.

events.title: Four survivors freed
events.detail: The official rescue summary says all four had been rescued from the wreckage by this time.
events.caption: All four survivors had been freed from the wreckage.

events.title: Survivors leave the crash site
events.detail: All four left the site aboard a Ground Self-Defense Force helicopter for onward medical treatment.
events.caption: A military helicopter carried all four survivors away for medical treatment.

events.title: Final report is published
events.detail: On 19 June 1987, AAIC published its report. It attributed the accident to bulkhead rupture caused by fatigue after the improper repair, followed by loss of tail structure and primary hydraulic flight control.
events.caption: Investigators linked an incorrect repair to cracking, pressure wall failure, and loss of tail and hydraulic control.

events.title: JTSB explains disputed issues
events.detail: In July 2011, JTSB issued an explanation addressing decompression, alternative causes, seabed searches and rescue. It acknowledged gaps in the original explanation and rescue documentation.
events.caption: Safety investigators addressed disputed issues and acknowledged gaps in earlier explanations and rescue records.

events.title: Reopening discussed in the Diet
events.detail: On 2 April 2025, the JTSB chair told a parliamentary committee that the official causal wording expressed a strong inference. He said the unidentified seabed object did not justify reopening.
events.caption: The safety board said an unidentified seabed object did not justify reopening the investigation.

events.title: Repair explanation remains unresolved
events.detail: On 28 October 2026, MLIT published Boeing and FAA replies about website statements on the repair. Boeing said there were no new facts; FAA offered no information beyond its webpage.
events.caption: Boeing reported no new repair facts; the aviation regulator supplied no additional information.

perspectives.label: Improper repair and fatigue
perspectives.held_by: AAIC; retained by JTSB and summarized by FAA
perspectives.claim: An improperly made 1978 bulkhead splice concentrated load in a single rivet row. Fatigue cracks grew until the bulkhead ruptured; escaping cabin air damaged the aft structure and vertical fin, and hydraulic losses removed primary flight control.

evidence_for.text: Recovered bulkhead fractures showed fatigue at the improperly repaired splice; the physical repair differed from the written instruction.
Recorded motion, aft-structure damage and reconstructed cabin-air flow support the sequence. Detached fin and aft-fuselage debris were recovered from Sagami Bay.

evidence_against.text: Not all tail wreckage was recovered. The complete human explanation of why the repair work departed from instructions remains undocumented in the material obtained.
Some critics question decompression because occupants did not recall violent wind or cold; JTSB explains why those experiences do not exclude a brief pressure loss.

ending.description: Loss of conventional control, oscillating flight, and a final right turn into successive ridges. Final-rest time is not fixed to a precise second.

perspectives.label: Flutter before bulkhead failure
perspectives.held_by: Critics described and answered in JTSB's 2011 explanatory document
perspectives.claim: This view proposes that structural weakness or flutter first damaged the vertical fin, with the bulkhead damage occurring later. It questions a rapid-decompression interpretation of the cabin observations.

evidence_for.text: Survivor recollections emphasized a brief sound and mist, without the sustained wind or severe cold some expected; flight crew did not visibly adopt the full decompression procedure.

evidence_against.text: AAIC found no recorder or wreckage pattern supporting flutter or divergence. JTSB notes that masks, mist, pressure indications and internally directed structural damage require explanation under this view.
A transient pressure loss need not produce prolonged cabin wind or immediately recognized symptoms; the repaired splice had physical fatigue evidence.

ending.description: No independently quantified alternative final path was found. This hypothesis changes the initiating failure, not an established alternative impact site.

perspectives.label: External object or missile
perspectives.held_by: Writer Tohko Aoyama and other external-object proponents; described critically in s3 and discussed by Tomotsune
perspectives.claim: Proponents suggest collision with a military target aircraft or missile, sometimes linked to allegations of concealment. No verified foreign object or explosive evidence establishing that cause was found in the sources examined.

evidence_for.text: Advocates rely on interpretations of witness accounts, an allegedly red or orange object, missing tail wreckage and gaps in disclosure. The 2026 campaign continues to seek raw records and reinvestigation.

evidence_against.text: JTSB identifies the red object cited in this argument as part of the main wing. Tests on about 160 wreckage specimens found no tested explosive substances or blast traces.

Physical fatigue at the defective splice, recorder evidence and inside-to-outside fin damage support the official mechanism. The 2025 JTSB testimony does not identify the seabed object as aircraft debris.

ending.description: No reproducible alternate track with sourced timestamps or a different crash site was found. Alleged additional airborne events are not animated as fact.

perspectives.label: Earlier rescue was possible
perspectives.held_by: Former USAF navigator Michael Antonucci; some survivors, families and later critics
perspectives.claim: Antonucci recalled that US helicopter personnel offered to descend nearby but were ordered away. This is a credible issue for rescue-history review; the number of additional people an earlier response could have saved is not established.

evidence_for.text: The official report independently confirms the C-130 fire report at about 19:15. Antonucci's later first-person account describes a helicopter and a return order.
Later accounts of a surviving off-duty cabin attendant describe breathing or voices after impact. JTSB acknowledges that rescue documentation was limited.

evidence_against.text: JTSB documents differing location reports and failed ground guidance; it describes serious hazards for night helicopter rescue in forested, uneven terrain.
The original US mission log and command order were not obtained. The report's medical findings do not establish how many additional people, if any, would have survived an earlier arrival.

ending.description: The flight and impact path are unchanged. This view concerns rescue after the crash, not a separate cause or destination.

evidence_points.label: Main crash ridge
evidence_points.detail: Approximate transformed report coordinate; original 35°59′54″N 138°41′49″E. The datum assumption is described in site. Wreckage spread across the ridge and adjacent ravines.

evidence_points.label: Yokota Air Base
evidence_points.detail: Current airport reference point, shown as rescue and communications context. It is not a reconstructed TACAN antenna coordinate or a search-aircraft position.

witnesses.who: Four ground witnesses south-southwest of the crash area
witnesses.said: Careful paraphrase: they saw a low, slow aircraft arriving from the Oku-Tama direction, then a sharp turn near the mountains and disappearance behind terrain. Their exact observation coordinates were not obtained.

witnesses.who: Captain of another airliner near Otsuki
witnesses.said: Careful paraphrase: the upper part of Mount Fuji was visible and there were no clouds between about 10,000 and 25,000 ft on the relevant route.

Careful paraphrase of a later account reproduced in s12: a brief noise, dropped oxygen masks, slight ear blockage and transient white mist. The same secondary account reports breathing nearby after the crash; it does not establish a count of potentially rescuable people.

Careful paraphrase of Antonucci's 1995 account as reproduced in s12: the crew located the fire, directed a Marine helicopter and later received a return-to-base order. This retrospective account was not checked against original mission or command logs.

why_it_matters: The accident led to changes protecting 747 tail structure and hydraulic systems from pressure-bulkhead failure, improved bulkhead inspection, and stronger attention to repair assessment and damage tolerance (s1, s5). JAL preserves wreckage and uses the accident in staff safety education (s15).

conflicts.b: Attachment 5 says about 5,000 ft. Both are recorder-related pressure-altitude descriptions; neither is selected.
Attachment 5 places it at 18:55:42 JST. The point and event use the main-text time with this disagreement explicit.

conflicts.a: Attachment 5 gives leading-edge extension beginning at 18:51:06 JST.
conflicts.b: Section 3.1.7.4 refers to flap operation from about 18:51:14. These may describe different aspects of the sequence; no silent correction is made.

conflicts.about: When the crash site was confirmed
conflicts.a: The 1987 report calls the 04:39 military observation a site confirmation and gives 05:37 for police confirmation.
conflicts.b: JTSB's 2011 Table 3 plots the 04:39 location about 3 km from the site. Airborne sighting, a radio fix, and ground access are different milestones.

conflicts.a: Antonucci's later account says a US helicopter was ready to lower personnel nearby when ordered to leave.
conflicts.b: JTSB describes position errors, night-flight hazards and limited documentation. The original US operational record and proof of how many additional lives could have been saved were not obtained.

conflicts.about: Why Boeing's repair team used a divided splice
conflicts.a: FAA teaching material attributes the divided plate to installation difficulty; a 2026 news report says Boeing removed similar wording and apologized for confusion.
conflicts.b: The 1987 investigation establishes the physical error but does not establish the full human decision process. On 28 October 2026 MLIT reported that Boeing claimed no new facts and FAA had no additional information.

conflicts.a: Critics argue that the absence of remembered violent wind or cold and the crew's mask behaviour contradict a rapid pressure loss.
conflicts.b: JTSB explains these experiences as compatible with a brief decompression and points to masks, mist, structural damage and recorder evidence. Recollection is not a cabin-pressure recording.

unknowns: No machine-readable decoded DFDR sample file, original radar-coordinate series, or full ATC surveillance tape was obtained. The available numeric commentary and scanned plots were inspected; do not treat the resulting sparse fields as a continuous measured trajectory.

The track deliberately extends the requested shape with pressure_alt_ft and cas_kt. ALT1 is pressure altitude and CAS1 is calibrated airspeed; true MSL flight altitude and IAS were not recovered at each timestamp, so alt_ft and ias_kt remain null. No pressure-to-geometric-altitude or CAS-to-IAS conversion is invented.

The final-path map is a published AAIC reconstruction. The datum is not explicitly identified on the inspected figure; Tokyo Datum is an assumption based on the map date and Japanese mapping history. The WGS84 conversion and manually digitized points are approximate. Round-off to 0.001 degree is not a confidence radius; final ridge contact points require finer surveyed georeferencing before close-up animation.

Before 18:46:03 JST no gridded geographic path was digitized. The general map in Attached Figure 1 was inspected, but its schematic line was not turned into invented precise coordinates. Earlier track positions are null.

Even after 18:46:03, recorder attitude points with no independently matching model timestamp keep their coordinates null. Do not merge or interpolate them as if a complete six-degree-of-freedom recorder solution existed.

Exact final-rest time is unknown here. The last analysable DFDR set at 18:56:27.25 JST, first tree contact and later terrain contacts are distinct events. The report gives an overall impact minute, not an independently synchronized final-rest instant.

Exact nose-gear state at every point, full individual engine thrust histories, geometric MSL heights, ground speed, wind corrections and angle of attack at most timestamps were not extracted. No values are carried forward merely to fill the schema.

The requested final-minute density is limited by plotted rather than tabulated records. Only selected onset plot values were digitized; final attitudes and other numerical points come from the report's explicit DFDR commentary. Plot readings are approximate and must not be displayed with raw-sample precision.

Historical airport reference-point elevations and coordinates of each 1985 planned navigation fix were not verified. Current facility coordinates are supplied for Haneda and Itami only; historical airport elevations and waypoint coordinates are null.

Cloud tops, site-specific cloud layers, visibility, wind, temperature, turbulence, lightning, moon visibility and weather in individual ravines were not found. Airport cloud-height datum is unspecified; observations are not a measured weather field along the path. No sea-state observation was found.
Two flap times and conflicting late-flight altitude descriptions remain explicit in conflicts; the Japanese original controls if the tentative English translation differs.

The original Pacific Stars and Stripes page of 27 August 1995, C-130 mission log, helicopter crew log, command-post recording and written withdrawal order were not obtained. Antonucci is cited through the identified reproduction, without treating it as a declassified military record.

The number, identities and potential survival time of people who may have remained alive after impact cannot be established from the material obtained. No numerical claim that a particular number would have been saved is made.

Not all detached vertical-fin, rudder and aft-body debris was recovered. A later reported seabed object remains unidentified in the official 2025 testimony; its coordinates, dimensions and relationship to JA8119 are not asserted.

The precise reason individual repair workers departed from instructions is still not established by the sources obtained. The 2024-2026 web explanations, withdrawal and October 2026 official replies do not supply a new documented interview or original work record.
No reopened investigation or new official causal finding was found in searches covering 2024 through 7 November 2026. Continuing advocacy is documented separately from established physical evidence.

An accident-day colour photograph or paint record establishing every marking was not obtained. Livery notes use a specifically dated 1984 photograph and do not establish every decal on the accident date.
memorial_note: This flight carried 509 passengers and 15 crew members; 520 people died, and four passengers survived.
